# Status report: jf2 allocator test on kestrel, 2026-11-20

## Short version

We tested whether jf2 (our fork of the jemalloc memory allocator) reduces the p99 latency spikes in kestrel (our key-value store) under one read-mostly workload. With jf2, p99 latency (the value that 99% of requests stay at or below) fell from 2140 us (microseconds) to 870 us (-59%), and throughput and median latency showed no measurable change. jf2 used 5.7 GB more memory (+9.3%), and the capacity team must approve that before we enable jf2 in staging (the pre-production environment).

## Words used here

- **jemalloc**: the memory allocator library that kestrel uses today, version 5.3.
- **Build A / Build B**: kestrel with jemalloc 5.3 / kestrel with jf2.
- **ycsb-b, ycsb-a**: workloads of YCSB (Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark). ycsb-b is read-mostly (95% reads, 5% updates). ycsb-a is write-heavy (50% reads, 50% updates).
- **p50, p99, p99.9 latency**: the latency that 50%, 99%, or 99.9% of requests stay at or below.
- **Latency spike**: a short period with latency far above normal.
- **kops/s**: thousand operations per second.
- **RSS**: resident set size, the physical memory the process holds.
- **Decay purge**: the step where jemalloc returns unused memory to the operating system after a delay.
- **perf**: the Linux profiler.
- **je_arena_decay**: a jemalloc function in the decay-purge code.
- **NUMA pinning**: binding the process to the cores and memory of one CPU socket.

## Test setup

- **Host**: bench-07, 2 x 32-core Xeon (64 cores), 512 GB RAM, Linux kernel 6.8.
- **System load**: load average 0.4 before the runs (near idle on 64 cores).
- **Build A**: commit 4f1c2aa on the main branch, with jemalloc 5.3.
- **Build B**: the same commit plus jf2. The allocator is the only difference.
- **Workload**: ycsb-b, 64 client threads, 10 min per run.
- **Runs**: 5 per build, alternating A, B, A, B.

## Results

```
p99 and p99.9 latency, median of 5 runs (1 block = 200 us)

p99    A ███████████ 2140 us
       B ████ 870 us                  (-59%)

p99.9  A █████████████████████████████████████████████████ 9800 us
       B ████████████████ 3100 us     (-68%)
```

Bars are rounded to the nearest block. Only the two high-percentile metrics moved.

Values are the median of 5 runs, with min..max in parentheses.

| Metric | A: jemalloc 5.3 | B: jf2 | Change, B vs A |
|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput, kops/s | 412 (405..418) | 409 (401..415) | -3 (-0.7%) |
| p50 latency, us | 118 (116..121) | 119 (117..121) | +1 (+0.8%) |
| p99 latency, us | 2140 (1890..2610) | 870 (820..940) | -1270 (-59%) |
| p99.9 latency, us | 9800 (7200..14100) | 3100 (2700..3900) | -6700 (-68%) |
| RSS at end of run, GB | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 (+9.3%) |

## What the data shows

- **High-percentile latency dropped.** On both metrics, the highest B value is below the lowest A value [p99: B max 940 us, A min 1890 us; p99.9: B max 3900 us, A min 7200 us].
- **B varies less between runs.** The p99 spread over 5 runs was 720 us for A and 120 us for B [p99 row, max minus min].
- **Throughput and p50 did not change measurably.** The differences are -0.7% and +0.8%, and the A and B ranges overlap [throughput and p50 rows].
- **Memory use went up.** RSS at the end of the run was 5.7 GB higher with B [RSS row]. Only one value per build was recorded, so the run-to-run spread of RSS is unknown.

## Likely cause of the spikes in build A

The decay purge is the likely cause.

- The spikes in A occur at the same times as the decay purge [spike timeline, build A].
- In the spike windows, 31% of perf samples were inside je_arena_decay [perf profile, build A].
- Build B runs the purge in a background thread, and its p99 is 59% lower [p99 row]. This is consistent with the purge being the cause.
- Insufficient data: the je_arena_decay share outside the spike windows was not recorded. That number would show how far 31% is above the normal level.

## Deviation from the plan

- Run 3 of build B had a 40 s stall at minute 7 of the 10 min run.
- We traced the stall to logrotate (the log-file rotation tool), which the nightly cron job (the system scheduler) started. The allocator did not cause it.
- We repeated the run. The results above use the repeat and exclude the stalled run.

## Not tested

- ycsb-a (the write-heavy workload).
- More than 64 client threads.
- NUMA pinning.

The results apply only to ycsb-b at 64 client threads without NUMA pinning.

## Open decision

Is the RSS increase of 5.7 GB (+9.3%) acceptable? The capacity team must decide.

## Next steps

1. Run ycsb-a tomorrow (2026-11-21).
2. Ask the capacity team for a decision on the RSS increase.
3. If they approve, enable jf2 in staging, controlled by a configuration flag.

---

Notes for you, not part of the report:

- **YCSB mixes**: the 95/5 and 50/50 read/update splits are the standard YCSB definitions, not from your notes. Check that they match your configuration.
- **Computed values**: I calculated the percent changes and the p99 spreads from your medians and ranges.
- **Tomorrow's run**: 2026-11-21 is a Saturday, and the nightly logrotate can stall the ycsb-a run the same way. Consider pausing that cron job during the runs.
